paper_topic: SCDS — a state-only framework for learning Contractive Dynamical System policies for imitation learning, using recurrent equilibrium networks + coupling layers to guarantee contractivity for any parameter choice and enable efficient out-of-sample recovery

nodes.text: Imitation learning provides an intuitive policy optimization framework for executing complex robotic tasks by learning from expert demonstrations (Hussein et al., 2017).
However, naively replicating expert behavior can raise safety concerns during deployment, as the robot's trajectory may become unreliable when facing out-of-sample (OOS) states.
nodes.display_label: Naive imitation unreliable on OOS states

nodes.text: For instance, if the robot begins from an unknown initial state or encounters environmental perturbations, it could fail to maintain a consistent and reliable behavior.
To address this issue, the policy can be modeled using a dynamical system (DS) with rigorous reliability certificates (Ravichandar et al., 2020; Dawson et al., 2023).
nodes.display_label: Model policy as DS with certificates

nodes.text: One such certificate is asymptotic stability (Devaney, 2021), which ensures that all trajectories eventually converge to the same equilibrium state, regardless of the initial condition or perturbations (Khansari-Zadeh & Billard, 2011; Rana et al., 2020; Abyaneh et al., 2024).
While asymptotic stability guarantees convergence, it overlooks the transient behavior (Tsukamoto et al., 2021).
This phenomenon is illustrated in Fig. 1 for an arbitrary OOS initial state, where the trajectory induced by the stable policy converges to the target but fails to imitate the expert.
nodes.display_label: Stable trajectory fails to imitate expert

nodes.text: Fig. 1

In contrast, contractive DS policies ensure that the resulting trajectories exponentially converge to each other, and ultimately to the equilibrium state (Ravichandar et al., 2017; Mohammadi et al., 2024).
nodes.display_label: Contractive DS: trajectories converge to each other

nodes.text: We leverage the stronger notion of contractivity (Lohmiller & Slotine, 1998) to ensure reliability in the transient phase, and as a result, enhance the imitation quality.
There are two main approaches to learning contractive DSs.
nodes.display_label: Two approaches to contractive DS learning

nodes.text: The most common method relies on constrained optimization to train the DS while satisfying learned or fixed contractivity certificates (Ravichandar et al., 2017; Blocher et al., 2017; Sindhwani et al., 2018).
However, constrained optimization is computationally challenging for complex expert behaviors or high-dimensional state spaces.
Additionally, most constrained approaches trade off imitation accuracy for constraint satisfaction.
The second approach is based on parameterized models with built-in contractivity guarantees for any choice of parameters (Mohammadi et al., 2024; Dawson et al., 2023).
As a result, the model remains contractive even if the learning process is imperfect or disrupted.
nodes.display_label: Model stays contractive under imperfect training

nodes.text: In this work, we build on the foundation of two such formulations: (i) a parameterization of contractive continuous-time DSs using recurrent equilibrium networks (RENs) (Martinelli et al., 2023), and (ii) the coupling layer architecture (Papamakarios et al., 2021).
The former ensures that the DS is contractive with an adjustable rate, while the latter provides a trainable bijective transformation that preserves contraction properties.
nodes.display_label: RENs: adjustable rate; coupling: contraction-preserving bijection

nodes.text: Our experiments demonstrate that the coupling layers enhance the model's representation power, leading to improved imitation accuracy and faster training, while maintaining the contractive nature of the DS.
Contributions. We propose a State-only framework for learning Contractive Dynamical System policies (SCDS), which offers several distinct advantages.
First, SCDS learns the policy solely from state measurements, eliminating the need to measure the expert's velocity.

Hence, we address the cumulative error problem observed in previous methods that replicate expert velocity, where small errors can accumulate and lead to significant deviations in state space trajectories (Ravichandar et al., 2020; Abyaneh et al., 2024).
Additionally, SCDS enables learning in a latent space, with its dimension adapting to the problem at hand.

It facilitates learning in high-dimensional state spaces by mapping to lower-dimensional latent representations, while also providing flexibility in low-dimensional spaces through higher-dimensional embeddings.
From a theoretical standpoint, we provide a rigorous solution for OOS recovery by establishing an upper bound on the worst-case deviation from expert trajectories.
SCDS also offers control over the transient behavior through an adjustable and learnable contraction rate.
Training SCDS is highly efficient by relying on unconstrained optimization and neural ordinary differential equations (ODE) fixed-point differentiation for gradient computation (Chen et al., 2018).

observations:
ContractivePolicy's intro is a method-paper template with an unusually rich Limitation cluster across two distinct Prior_Work axes. Para 1 (N1-N3) sets up imitation learning Context and the OOS-state safety concern. The first Prior_Work pair (N4-N5) introduces dynamical-system policies with asymptotic-stability certificates; the immediate Limitation pair (N6-N7) critiques stability for ignoring transient behavior, with a Proof pointer to Fig. 1 illustrating the stable-vs-contractive rollout difference. The second Prior_Work (N8) introduces contractive DS as the stronger alternative.

The related-work block (N10-N12) is structurally interesting: it splits into two sub-approaches (A: constrained optimization, B: built-in contractivity parameterization), each with its own Limitation chain. Approach A gets two specific Limitations (N11a: computationally challenging, N11b: accuracy-vs-constraint trade-off). Approach B (N10b) is the foundation the paper builds on (N12).

Method block (N13-N15) introduces the SCDS hybrid of RENs + coupling layers; the Contribution block (N16 + 7 sub-claims a-g) is the longest in any of the seven papers, and is decomposed into a parent + 7 sub-claim children with elaboration edges to keep them grouped (N16b is an elaboration of N16a, N16d of N16c). Cross-segment addresses edges: N16e (worst-case deviation bound) and N16f (adjustable contraction rate) both address N6 (stability ignores transient behavior) — the upper bound and the rate are precisely the transient-control primitives the Limitation called out. N16g (unconstrained optimization + neural-ODE) addresses N11a (constrained optimization is computationally hard).
